theory.overview: Cryptographic hash functions are the fingerprint generators of the digital world—they produce fixed-size, unique representations of arbitrary data. Give a hash function the complete works of Shakespeare or a single character, and both produce outputs of identical length (256 bits for SHA-256). Unlike encryption, hashing is one-way: you cannot recover the input from the output. This property enables password storage, digital signatures, blockchain consensus, and data integrity verification. A good hash function guarantees that any change to input, however small, produces a completely different hash (avalanche effect), and finding two inputs with the same hash is computationally impossible (collision resistance).

sections.title: Properties of Cryptographic Hash Functions
sections.content: Five properties define cryptographic strength. Pre-image resistance: given hash h, finding any message m where hash(m) = h should be infeasible—this makes hashing one-way. Second pre-image resistance: given message m1, finding different m2 with same hash should be infeasible—prevents forging documents with identical hashes. Collision resistance: finding any m1, m2 where hash(m1) = hash(m2) should be infeasible—prevents attackers from creating malicious files with valid hashes. Avalanche effect: changing one input bit should change ~50% of output bits—ensures hashes look completely random. Determinism: same input always produces same output—enables verification. These properties collectively make hash functions foundationally secure.
keyPoints: Pre-image resistance: one-way, can't reverse hash
Second pre-image resistance: can't find alternative with same hash
Collision resistance: can't find any two inputs with same hash
Avalanche effect: small input change → completely different output

sections.title: SHA-2 Family
sections.content: SHA-256 and SHA-512, designed by NSA and published by NIST in 2001, dominate modern cryptography. SHA-256 produces 256-bit (32-byte) outputs and processes data in 512-bit blocks through 64 rounds of bit manipulation. The algorithm uses modular addition, bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, NOT), and circular shifts. A compression function updates eight 32-bit state variables (a-h) using message schedule words derived from input blocks. SHA-512 uses 64-bit words and 80 rounds for increased security. No practical collision attacks exist against SHA-2. SHA-256 secures Bitcoin, TLS certificates, and countless systems. SHA-384 and SHA-224 provide variants for specific use cases requiring different output sizes.
keyPoints: Uses bitwise ops, modular addition, and circular shifts
Eight working variables updated each round
No practical attacks despite intensive cryptanalysis

sections.title: Applications and Use Cases
sections.content: Hash functions enable diverse security applications. Password storage: systems store hash(password) instead of plaintext, verifying by re-hashing and comparing. Digital signatures: sign the hash of a message rather than the message itself—faster and produces fixed-size input for signature algorithms. Data integrity: include hash with downloads so users verify file wasn't corrupted or tampered. Blockchains: each block contains the previous block's hash, creating an immutable chain—changing any block would change all subsequent hashes. Message authentication codes (HMAC): combine hash with secret key to authenticate message origin. Commitment schemes: reveal hash of a secret now, disclose the secret later—proves you knew it beforehand without revealing it.
keyPoints: Digital signatures on fixed-size message digests

sections.title: Hash Attacks and Security
sections.content: Hash security degrades when weaknesses emerge. MD5, once ubiquitous, fell to practical collisions in 2004—never use it for security. SHA-1, which succeeded MD5, succumbed to collision attacks by 2017; major browsers now reject SHA-1 certificates. The birthday paradox governs collision probability: with n-bit hashes, random collisions become likely after 2^(n/2) attempts (square root of hash space). For SHA-256, this means 2^128 operations—beyond any foreseeable capability. However, quantum computers using Grover's algorithm could theoretically find collisions in 2^(n/3) operations, suggesting we may eventually need larger hashes. Post-quantum cryptography research explores 384+ bit hashes for long-term security.
keyPoints: Birthday attack: find collisions in 2^(n/2) operations
SHA-256 remains secure; consider SHA-3 or 384+ bits for quantum resistance

steps.title: Initialize State
steps.description: Set up initial hash values (IV) and constants derived from fractional parts of cube roots of first primes.
steps.latex: h0..h7 = initial values (first 32 bits of sqrt(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19))

steps.title: Preprocess Message
steps.description: Pad message to multiple of 512 bits: append '1', then '0's, then original length as 64-bit integer.

steps.title: Process Message Block
steps.description: Break message into 512-bit blocks. For each block, create message schedule of 64 words.
steps.latex: W[0..15] = block chunks, W[16..63] = σ functions

steps.title: Initialize Working Variables
steps.description: Copy current hash values into working variables a through h.
steps.latex: a=h0, b=h1, c=h2, d=h3, e=h4, f=h5, g=h6, h=h7

steps.title: Compression Function Round
steps.description: Perform 64 rounds of updates using message schedule word, round constant, and bitwise operations.
steps.latex: T1 = h + Σ1(e) + Ch(e,f,g) + K[i] + W[i]\T2 = Σ0(a) + Maj(a,b,c)\h = g, g = f, f = e, e = d + T1, d = c, c = b, b = a, a = T1 + T2

steps.title: Update Hash Values
steps.description: Add working variables back to hash values (modular addition).

steps.title: Produce Final Hash
steps.description: Concatenate all hash values to produce 256-bit digest.

practiceProblems.title: Hash Lengths
practiceProblems.description: What is the output size in bits of MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512?
hints: SHA-1: Secure Hash Algorithm 1 - produces 160 bits
SHA-256: the number indicates output bits

solution.explanation: The output size is often in the name. MD5 produces 128 bits (16 bytes), SHA-1 produces 160 bits (20 bytes), SHA-256 produces 256 bits (32 bytes), and SHA-512 produces 512 bits (64 bytes).

practiceProblems.title: Birthday Attack
practiceProblems.description: Approximately how many random SHA-256 hashes must be generated before finding a collision with 50% probability?
hints: Birthday paradox applies: square root of search space

solution.explanation: Due to the birthday paradox, collisions become likely after generating approximately √(2^256) = 2^128 hashes. This is far beyond any computational capability.

practiceProblems.title: Avalanche Effect
practiceProblems.description: You hash 'Hello' and 'hello' (only first letter changed). What percentage of output bits typically differ?
hints: Avalanche effect: small input change → large output change
Good hash functions aim for ~50% bit flips

solution.explanation: In a well-designed hash function, changing one bit of input should flip about half the output bits on average. This makes it impossible to predict output changes from input changes.

practiceProblems.title: Password Storage
practiceProblems.description: Why do secure systems store hash(password + salt) instead of hash(password) or the password itself?
practiceProblems.latex: store: hash(password || salt), verify: hash(input || salt) == stored
hints: Plaintext passwords: catastrophic if database leaks
Salt: random value per user, prevents precomputed attacks

solution.answer: Hashing prevents recovering plaintext; salt prevents rainbow table attacks by ensuring same passwords produce different hashes
solution.explanation: Storing hash(password) without salt allows attackers to use precomputed rainbow tables. Adding a unique salt per user forces attackers to crack each password individually. Using slow hash functions (bcrypt, Argon2) further increases cracking cost.

practiceProblems.title: Blockchain Chaining
practiceProblems.description: How does including the previous block's hash in the current block create an immutable chain?
hints: Each block references previous by hash
Changing any block changes its hash

solution.answer: Any modification changes that block's hash, which doesn't match the stored hash in the next block, breaking the chain
solution.explanation: This creates a tamper-evident structure. To change an old block without detection, an attacker must recompute all subsequent blocks' hashes and outpace honest miners (computationally infeasible in proof-of-work systems).

practiceProblems.title: Pre-image Resistance
practiceProblems.description: Given a SHA-256 hash output h, how difficult is it to find any message m such that SHA-256(m) = h?
practiceProblems.latex: Given h, find m: SHA-256(m) = h. Complexity: O(2^256)
hints: This is the definition of pre-image resistance
Only option is trying all possible inputs

solution.answer: It requires approximately 2^256 attempts on average (computationally impossible)
solution.explanation: Pre-image resistance guarantees that even if you know the hash, you cannot find any input that produces it without brute force. For SHA-256, this is 2^256 operations—more than all the computing power in the world could accomplish in the age of the universe.

snippets.title: SHA-256 Hashing
snippets.code:
import hashlib

# Basic string hashing
message = b"Hello, World!"
hash_obj = hashlib.sha256(message)
hash_hex = hash_obj.hexdigest()

print(f"Message: {message}")
print(f"SHA-256: {hash_hex}")
print(f"Length: {len(hash_hex)} chars = {len(hash_hex)//2} bytes")

# Hashing file
with open("file.txt", "rb") as f:
    file_hash = hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()
    print(f"\nFile hash: {file_hash}")

# Demonstrating avalanche effect
msg1 = b"Hello"
msg2 = b"hello"  # Different case
print(f"\n{msg1}: {hashlib.sha256(msg1).hexdigest()[:16]}...")
print(f"{msg2}: {hashlib.sha256(msg2).hexdigest()[:16]}...")
# Completely different outputs!

snippets.title: Password Hashing with Salt
snippets.code:
import hashlib
import os
import hmac

def hash_password(password: str, salt: bytes = None) -> tuple:
    """Secure password hashing with salt"""
    if salt is None:
        salt = os.urandom(32)  # 256-bit random salt
    
    # Use PBKDF2 for key stretching (100k iterations)
    pwd_hash = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac(
        'sha256',              # Hash function
        password.encode(),     # Password bytes
        salt,                  # Salt
        100000                 # Iterations
    )
    return salt, pwd_hash

# Store password
password = "user_password123"
salt, pwd_hash = hash_password(password)
print(f"Salt: {salt.hex()[:32]}...")
print(f"Hash: {pwd_hash.hex()[:32]}...")

# Verify password
def verify_password(password: str, salt: bytes, stored_hash: bytes) -> bool:
    _, computed = hash_password(password, salt)
    return hmac.compare_digest(computed, stored_hash)

is_valid = verify_password("user_password123", salt, pwd_hash)
print(f"\nPassword valid: {is_valid}")  # True
